screens.title: Physical Backups with Percona XtraBackup
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn when and why to choose physical, hot backups for MySQL, and how Percona XtraBackup implements them for InnoDB. We begin with the core idea: copying raw data files and associated transaction log information is far faster than exporting millions of rows as S Q L statements. That speed matters when you manage large datasets or must meet strict recovery time objectives. You will see the typical workflow: install XtraBackup, run a non-blocking backup, execute the mandatory prepare step to apply redo logs, and then copy the prepared files back to the server for restoration. Along the way we surface common pitfalls: forgetting to prepare the backup, incorrect file permissions, insufficient disk space, and mismatched MySQL configuration. The chapter gives concrete terminal commands for a full backup and restore, and a hands-on activity that walks you through backing up and restoring a sample sales database. By the end you should be able to choose XtraBackup for large deployments, run a safe backup, and restore to a consistent state. Consider this question as you begin: how does applying redo logs during prepare change the shape of raw copied files into a usable data set?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Physical Backups Overview
Physical Backups with Percona XtraBackup
Understand hot backups, prepare and restore workflows that minimize downtime for large MySQL deployments.
This lesson focuses on why physical backups are faster for very large datasets, how a hot backup captures the LSN and redo logs for consistency, and the practical steps to back up and restore using XtraBackup. You will also learn everyday safety checks and common pitfalls to avoid when managing physical backup files.
In this lesson
  • Why physical backups beat logical exports at scale.
  • How InnoDB hot backups capture data plus redo logs.
  • Step-by-step XtraBackup commands for backup, prepare, and restore.
Explore Key Topics
Hot Backup
Copy files while server runs; captures LSN and redo.
Prepare Step
Apply redo logs to make files consistent before restore.
Restore
Copy prepared files back, fix permissions, and start MySQL.
Visual concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Backup
xtrabackup --backup + target-dir captures data files and binlog position.
LSN & Redo
LSN snapshot and redo logs are recorded for later prepare.
Prepare
xtrabackup --prepare applies redo, rolling forward committed changes.
Restore
xtrabackup --copy-back then fix ownership and start MySQL.
Key Takeaway

For very large MySQL deployments, hot physical backups with prepare provide fast backups and fast recovery, but they require careful preparation and validation.

Third, you will learn to run Percona XtraBackup to perform a non-blocking full backup, including how to select the target directory and required privileges. Finally, you will describe the prepare step and why it is necessary to apply redo logs to the copied files before attempting a restore. Each objective pairs explanation with a short verification task so you can confirm competency in a lab environment. screens.title: Physical vs Logical Backups
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare physical and logical backups and make the decision rules explicit. A logical backup like mysqldump exports table definitions and row data as S Q L statements. It's flexible and portable, but when your dataset grows to hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes that row-by-row export becomes slow and can impose heavy input and output on the production server. Physical backups copy raw files such as InnoDB tablespace files and redo logs. Because they operate at the filesystem level, they avoid per-row processing and can complete much faster. For example, restoring a multi-hundred-gigabyte dataset from a logical export requires replaying millions of inserts, while a physical restore is a file copy and permission fix. A common misconception is that physical backups are always riskier because they are less portable. The important contrast is that physical backups require awareness of MySQL configuration and matching environment details—datadir, innodb_log_file_size, and compatible MySQL versions—while logical backups are independent of those file-level settings. Practical guidance: choose mysqldump for small, portable exports or for migrating incompatible server versions; choose XtraBackup-style physical backups for large, mission-critical deployments where backup and restore speed and minimal downtime are primary concerns. To check your choice, estimate backup window and restore time for your data size and select the approach that meets your RTO and RPO.

keyIdea.text: Use physical backups for very large datasets when recovery speed and low impact on production matter; use logical exports for portability and small datasets.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Physical vs Logical
Logical Backup (mysqldump)
  • Exports schema and rows as SQL; highly portable across versions.
  • Good for small datasets, schema migrations, or when portability is required.
  • Becomes slow and resource-heavy for very large databases.
Common misconception

People assume logical exports are always safer; in large systems they can cause unacceptable downtime due to long restore times.

Physical Backup (XtraBackup / MEB)
  • Copies raw files and logs, enabling much faster backup and restore at filesystem speed.
  • Supports hot backups for InnoDB by capturing LSN and redo logs for later prepare.
  • Requires environment compatibility and correct prepare/restore steps to succeed.
Key Takeaway

For large data sets choose physical backups to meet tight RTOs, but plan config compatibility and verification steps.

screens.title: What is a Hot InnoDB Backup?
screens.narratorSegment: A hot backup for InnoDB is a process that produces a consistent copy of the database files while the server remains online and processing transactions. The key enabler is InnoDB's transactional architecture: committed changes are recorded in redo logs and tracked with a Log Sequence Number, or LSN. A hot backup tool copies the data files while also capturing the LSN and copies of the redo logs so the backup can be brought to a consistent state afterwards. Concretely, the backup contains file images plus the necessary redo information to roll forward committed transactions and roll back unfinished ones when you run the prepare step. An important misconception is to think a hot backup always avoids any input and output impact; in reality, while XtraBackup is non-blocking for data operations, it still consumes disk and C P U resources and requires appropriate privileges to read files safely. For example, during a full hot backup you will see XtraBackup record the binary log position in xtrabackup_binlog_info; that file is crucial if you need point-in-time recovery after restoring. The practical signal you should watch for is the LSN numbers reported by XtraBackup: they indicate how far redo needs to be applied during prepare. After you understand these pieces, the prepare step becomes less mysterious: it applies redo using those saved LSNs so the files represent a consistent committed state.

keyIdea.title: Hot backup essence
keyIdea.text: Hot backups capture both data files and redo/log metadata so a consistent state can be produced later without stopping the server.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Hot InnoDB Backup
Definition
A hot InnoDB backup copies raw files while the server is online, capturing the LSN and redo logs needed for later prepare.
Key points:
  • InnoDB transactions use redo logs to record committed changes.
  • A hot backup records the LSN and redo metadata alongside the copied files.
  • The prepare step uses those logs to make the copied files consistent.
Misconception

Hot means zero impact. In practice, hot backups still consume disk and CPU and require correct privileges; plan accordingly.

Annotated workflow
Snapshot files
xtrabackup copies table space files and .frm metadata while server writes concurrently.
Record LSN
The tool records the LSN and creates xtrabackup_binlog_info for binlog coordinates.
Prepare
Applying redo rolls forward committed transactions and removes uncommitted changes.
Restore
After copy-back and permission fixes, MySQL starts and performs normal crash recovery if needed.

screens.title: Percona XtraBackup at a glance
screens.narratorSegment: Percona XtraBackup is an open-source tool that implements hot physical backups for MySQL, with particular strength for InnoDB and support for MyISAM tables as well. It performs full, incremental, and differential backups by copying raw files, tracking LSNs, and recording binary log coordinates for point-in-time recovery. XtraBackup requires a user with specific privileges—RELOAD, PROCESS, LOCK TABLES, REPLICATION CLIENT, BINLOG ADMIN, and BACKUP_ADMIN—so it can safely read files and query the server for binlog positions. A common misconception is that installing XtraBackup alone is sufficient; in practice you must also ensure the data directory path is correct and that the server's configuration will allow files to be used on restore. Architecturally, XtraBackup works by coordinating a filesystem copy with metadata queries to ensure it captures the required log state. It writes progress and LSN information to the target directory; that metadata is required for the prepare step. For enterprise users there is a commercial counterpart, but for this chapter we focus on XtraBackup because it is widely used and accessible. Think of XtraBackup as a two-part system: a fast file copier and a metadata recorder that together make a consistent prepared image possible.

keyIdea.text: XtraBackup copies files and records metadata; it needs specific privileges and correct datadir to produce a usable backup.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Percona XtraBackup
Capabilities
  • Full, incremental, and differential physical backups for InnoDB and MyISAM.
  • Hot backup support via LSN capture and recording of binlog coordinates.
  • Prepare step to apply redo logs and produce a consistent image.
Required privileges
RELOAD, PROCESS, LOCK TABLES, REPLICATION CLIENT, BINLOG ADMIN, BACKUP_ADMIN. These let XtraBackup read server state and report binlog positions safely.
Architecture summary
XtraBackup copies files while querying the server for LSN and binlog positions, writing both files and metadata into the target directory for later prepare and restore.
Pro tip

Confirm --datadir matches the live MySQL data directory. A mismatch produces incomplete backups.

screens.title: Install and Prepare the Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Before running a backup you must prepare the server and environment. Start by installing Percona XtraBackup 8.0 on the server that runs MySQL 8.0. On Debian or Ubuntu you would use the package manager to install percona-xtrabackup-80; on RHEL or CentOS install the matching package. Next, create a dedicated backup user and grant the required privileges: RELOAD, PROCESS, LOCK TABLES, REPLICATION CLIENT, BINLOG ADMIN, and BACKUP_ADMIN. This separation reduces risk and keeps audit trails clear. Choose a target directory with ample free space—physical backups duplicate data at the filesystem level so the backup destination should be sized at least as large as your data directory plus headroom for the prepare step. Consider filesystem performance: a slow target can prolong backup windows. Finally, verify that the backup user can connect and that the MySQL datadir path you will pass to xtrabackup matches the server's configuration. A common mistake at this stage is assuming default paths; always verify /var/lib/mysql or your custom datadir before proceeding. These preparation steps reduce surprises during the actual backup and ensure the backup will be usable for prepare and restore.

keyIdea.title: Preparation matters
keyIdea.text: Install XtraBackup, create a dedicated backup user with required grants, and choose a properly sized target directory before running backups.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Install & Environment
Installation and user grants
  1. Install percona-xtrabackup-80 via your package manager on the MySQL host.
  2. Create a backup user and grant RELOAD, PROCESS, LOCK TABLES, REPLICATION CLIENT, BINLOG ADMIN, BACKUP_ADMIN.
  3. Verify connectivity and privilege checks by running a test command with that user.
Mnemonic: install, grant, verify.
Target directory & capacity
Create a timestamped directory for each backup and ensure free space equals at least the live data size plus headroom for prepare. For example, mkdir -p /data/backups/full_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).
Common mistake

Using an undersized or slow backup target prolongs backups and can cause prepare to fail due to insufficient temp space.

screens.title: Running a Full Backup with xtrabackup
screens.narratorSegment: Now let's walk through a concrete backup command and what each option does. You will create a timestamped target directory for clarity and retention. The primary command uses xtrabackup --backup with --target-dir to specify where the files will be saved, --user and --password for the backup user, and --datadir to indicate the live MySQL data directory. During the backup xtrabackup copies InnoDB files, MyISAM files, and records the binary log position into xtrabackup_binlog_info inside the target directory. A typical sequence is creating the directory, running xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/data/backups/full_backup_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS --user=backup_user --password=your_password --datadir=/var/lib/mysql, and waiting for completion. Monitor the output for LSN and confirmation of success. A common pitfall here is passing an incorrect datadir or using a user without required privileges—both lead to incomplete backups. After the backup completes the files exist in the target directory but are not prepared; they are a raw image requiring the next step. Practice: run the command on a test instance and inspect the target directory for xtrabackup_binlog_info and the backup files to validate a successful run. Running a Full Backup with xtrabackup means xtrabackup --backup with --target-dir and --datadir captures raw files and records binlog position; verify output and presence of metadata files.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › xtrabackup --backup
Starter commands (example)
# Create directory
mkdir -p /data/backups/full_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)

# Perform the backup
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/data/backups/full_backup_20220101_120000 \
  --user=backup_user --password=StrongPassword123! --datadir=/var/lib/mysql
Watch for progress, LSN values, and the creation of xtrabackup_binlog_info in the target directory.
What to check after backup
  • xtrabackup_binlog_info exists and contains binlog coordinates.
  • Backup finished without errors and reported final LSN.
  • Target directory has expected files and sufficient free space remained.
Danger

Do not attempt to restore from these raw files until you run xtrabackup --prepare.

screens.title: The Prepare Step Explained
screens.narratorSegment: The prepare step is the heart of converting a raw, hot backup into a consistent set of files suitable for restoration. When XtraBackup copies files from a running server it inevitably captures some pages that were in-flight: some transactions will be committed, some not. The prepare operation reads the redo logs and applies all committed transactions to the copied data files, rolling forward to the LSN recorded during the backup. It also undoes uncommitted transactions so the resulting files reflect a crash-consistent, committed-only state. Run xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/path/to/backup before any attempt to copy files back to a data directory. A common misconception is that MySQL's own crash recovery can substitute for prepare; while MySQL has crash recovery, it expects data files to be internally consistent with redo logs available. Without prepare, MySQL will likely fail to start or report corruption because the copied files themselves are incomplete. Practically, prepare may require additional temporary disk space because it may write intermediate data. After prepare completes, the backup directory contains prepared files that can be copied back safely. A short verification step is to inspect the prepare output for the final LSN and confirmation that the log apply finished successfully.

A common misconception is that MySQL's own crash recovery can substitute for prepare; while MySQL has crash recovery, it expects data files to be internally consistent with redo logs available. Without prepare, MySQL will likely fail to start or report corruption because the copied files themselves are incomplete. Practically, prepare may require additional temporary disk space because it may write intermediate data. After prepare completes, the backup directory contains prepared files that can be copied back safely. A short verification step is to inspect the prepare output for the final LSN and confirmation that the log apply finished successfully.

keyIdea.title: Prepare necessity
keyIdea.text: xtrabackup --prepare applies redo logs to create a crash-consistent image; skipping it commonly causes MySQL startup failures after restore.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Prepare Step
What prepare does
  • Reads redo logs saved during backup and applies committed transactions.
  • Rolls back any uncommitted transactions to produce a crash-consistent image.
  • Records final LSNs indicating the point to which logs were applied.
If you skip it

MySQL may fail to start or report corruption because the copied files are not consistent without applying redo.

Command
sudo xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/data/backups/full_backup_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS
Review output for LSN processed lines and a final confirmation that the backup is prepared.
Check

After prepare, the files in the target directory are ready for copy-back; confirm the final LSN and absence of errors in the prepare output.

screens.title: Restoring a Prepared Backup
screens.narratorSegment: Restoring from a prepared physical backup follows a deliberate sequence. First, stop the MySQL server so you can safely overwrite the data directory: sudo systemctl stop mysql. Optionally, clear the existing datadir if you intend a clean overwrite, but be extremely cautious: removing files is destructive. Next, execute xtrabackup --copy-back --target-dir=/path/to/prepared_backup --datadir=/var/lib/mysql to copy the prepared files into MySQL's data directory. After copy-back, fix ownership and permissions so the server can read and write the files: sudo chown -R mysql:mysql /var/lib/mysql and sudo chmod -R 750 /var/lib/mysql. Then start MySQL and allow it to perform normal crash recovery; it should come online with the restored data. A frequent mistake is copying unprepared files or forgetting to adjust ownership, which causes startup failures. For verification, log into MySQL and check the expected tables and data. In the hands-on activity you simulate data loss by dropping a table and then restoring; after the restore you confirm that pre-loss rows are present and that post-backup insertions are not. When restoring to a different server, ensure my. cnf settings like innodb_log_file_size are compatible to avoid startup mismatches.

keyIdea.title: Restore steps
keyIdea.text: Stop MySQL, copy prepared files back with xtrabackup --copy-back, set mysql:mysql ownership and correct permissions, then start and verify.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Restore Procedure
Step-by-step commands
# Stop MySQL
sudo systemctl stop mysql

# (Optional) Clear existing data - destructive
# sudo rm -rf /var/lib/mysql/*

# Copy prepared files back
sudo xtrabackup --copy-back --target-dir=/data/backups/full_backup_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS --datadir=/var/lib/mysql

# Fix permissions
sudo chown -R mysql:mysql /var/lib/mysql
sudo chmod -R 750 /var/lib/mysql

# Start MySQL
sudo systemctl start mysql
Verification checklist
  • MySQL process starts without corruption errors.
  • Expected tables and data are present; run SELECT checks.
  • Confirm xtrabackup_binlog_info if point-in-time recovery is needed.
Caution

Double-check you are restoring prepared files and not overwriting a live production directory unintentionally.

screens.title: Permissions, Configuration and LSNs
screens.narratorSegment: Several environment details influence whether a prepared backup will restore cleanly. First, datadir: the --datadir you pass to xtrabackup must point to the live MySQL data directory. If it does not, the backup will not contain correct files or the tool will copy the wrong set. Second, permissions and ownership are critical; after copy-back set the files to mysql:mysql and appropriate directory permissions, or MySQL will be unable to start. Third, the LSN recorded during backup and processed during prepare indicates how far redo must be applied. Inspecting the prepare output confirms which LSNs were processed and helps you reason about recovery point. Another important element is binary log position: xtrabackup writes xtrabackup_binlog_info with the binlog filename and position at backup time, which you will need for point-in-time recovery. A common misconception is that matching MySQL version alone guarantees success; in reality innodb_log_file_size and other innodb parameters should be compatible with the backup image. If these settings differ dramatically the server may not start or may require adjustments. In summary, pay attention to datadir, permissions, LSNs, binary log info, and configuration parity before performing a restore.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Permissions & LSNs
Datadir
Confirm --datadir points to the live MySQL data directory when running backups or copy-back operations.
Permissions
After copy-back set ownership to mysql:mysql and secure permissions so MySQL can read and write files.
LSN & Binlog
Inspect prepare output for final LSNs and review xtrabackup_binlog_info for binlog coordinates used in point-in-time recovery.
Practical check

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Working with physical backups introduces several common failure modes that you can avoid with deliberate checks. The most frequent error is forgetting to run xtrabackup --prepare before copy-back; without prepare the raw files are inconsistent and MySQL will likely fail. Another common issue is incorrect file ownership or permissions after copying files back; always chown mysql:mysql and set restrictive permissions. Ensure adequate disk space on the backup target and temporary space for prepare operations; lack of space can cause prepare to fail mid-way. Do not overwrite a live production data directory without absolute certainty; instead restore to a separate server for verification if possible. Keep backups organized with timestamped directories and retain xtrabackup_binlog_info for point-in-time needs. Also, routinely test restores: a backup that has never been restored is not fully validated. Finally, maintain configuration parity where possible: extreme changes to innodb_log_file_size or other critical innodb parameters between backup and restore can cause incompatibilities. Following these best practices—prepare, permission fixes, capacity checks, test restores, and configuration parity—substantially reduces the chance of a failed recovery when it matters most. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In this chapter you will learn when and why to choose physical, hot backups for MySQL, and how Percona XtraBackup implements them for InnoDB. We begin with the core idea: copying raw data files and associated transaction log information is far faster than exporting millions of rows as S Q L statements. That speed matters when you manage large datasets or must meet strict recovery time objectives. You will see the typical workflow: install XtraBackup, run a non-blocking backup, execute the mandatory prepare step to apply redo logs, and then copy the prepared files back to the server for restoration. Along the way we surface common pitfalls: forgetting to prepare the backup, incorrect file permissions, insufficient disk space, and mismatched MySQL configuration. The chapter gives concrete terminal commands for a full backup and restore, and a hands-on activity that walks you through backing up and restoring a sample sales database. By the end you should be able to choose XtraBackup for large deployments, run a safe backup, and restore to a consistent state. Consider this question as you begin: how does applying redo logs during prepare change the shape of raw copied files into a usable data set?

These objectives map to both conceptual understanding and practical skills. First, you'll explain the fundamental differences between physical and logical backups and why physical copies make sense for very large datasets. Second, you will understand what a hot InnoDB backup is: how it captures file images plus transaction log metadata while the server remains online. Third, you will learn to run Percona XtraBackup to perform a non-blocking full backup, including how to select the target directory and required privileges. Finally, you will describe the prepare step and why it is necessary to apply redo logs to the copied files before attempting a restore. Each objective pairs explanation with a short verification task so you can confirm competency in a lab environment. What you'll be able to do means combine conceptual knowledge about innodb hot backups with hands-on commands for backup and prepare.. In practical terms, knowledge and hands-on skills this chapter builds. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These second-tier objectives focus on safe execution and verification. You will learn to execute a full restore from a prepared backup, including stopping MySQL, copying files back, and fixing ownership and permissions so the server can start. You will also identify common pitfalls such as forgetting prepare, insufficient disk space, or overwriting live data accidentally. Additionally, you'll record and use the binary log position stored in xtrabackup_binlog_info to support point-in-time recovery scenarios. Finally, you'll practice a lab that creates a sample database, backs it up, simulates data loss, and verifies restoration by comparing pre- and post-restore contents. These objectives ensure you can both perform the commands and reason about the safety of each step. Practical skills and safety checks means master the restore steps, permission fixes, and verification needed to use physical backups in production safely.. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's compare physical and logical backups and make the decision rules explicit. A logical backup like mysqldump exports table definitions and row data as S Q L statements. It's flexible and portable, but when your dataset grows to hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes that row-by-row export becomes slow and can impose heavy input and output on the production server. Physical backups copy raw files such as InnoDB tablespace files and redo logs. Because they operate at the filesystem level, they avoid per-row processing and can complete much faster. For example, restoring a multi-hundred-gigabyte dataset from a logical export requires replaying millions of inserts, while a physical restore is a file copy and permission fix. A common misconception is that physical backups are always riskier because they are less portable. The important contrast is that physical backups require awareness of MySQL configuration and matching environment details—datadir, innodb_log_file_size, and compatible MySQL versions—while logical backups are independent of those file-level settings. Practical guidance: choose mysqldump for small, portable exports or for migrating incompatible server versions; choose XtraBackup-style physical backups for large, mission-critical deployments where backup and restore speed and minimal downtime are primary concerns. To check your choice, estimate backup window and restore time for your data size and select the approach that meets your RTO and RPO.

A hot backup for InnoDB is a process that produces a consistent copy of the database files while the server remains online and processing transactions. The key enabler is InnoDB's transactional architecture: committed changes are recorded in redo logs and tracked with a Log Sequence Number, or LSN. A hot backup tool copies the data files while also capturing the LSN and copies of the redo logs so the backup can be brought to a consistent state afterwards. Concretely, the backup contains file images plus the necessary redo information to roll forward committed transactions and roll back unfinished ones when you run the prepare step. An important misconception is to think a hot backup always avoids any input and output impact; in reality, while XtraBackup is non-blocking for data operations, it still consumes disk and C P U resources and requires appropriate privileges to read files safely. For example, during a full hot backup you will see XtraBackup record the binary log position in xtrabackup_binlog_info; that file is crucial if you need point-in-time recovery after restoring. The practical signal you should watch for is the LSN numbers reported by XtraBackup: they indicate how far redo needs to be applied during prepare. After you understand these pieces, the prepare step becomes less mysterious: it applies redo using those saved LSNs so the files represent a consistent committed state.

Percona XtraBackup is an open-source tool that implements hot physical backups for MySQL, with particular strength for InnoDB and support for MyISAM tables as well. It performs full, incremental, and differential backups by copying raw files, tracking LSNs, and recording binary log coordinates for point-in-time recovery. XtraBackup requires a user with specific privileges—RELOAD, PROCESS, LOCK TABLES, REPLICATION CLIENT, BINLOG ADMIN, and BACKUP_ADMIN—so it can safely read files and query the server for binlog positions. A common misconception is that installing XtraBackup alone is sufficient; in practice you must also ensure the data directory path is correct and that the server's configuration will allow files to be used on restore. Architecturally, XtraBackup works by coordinating a filesystem copy with metadata queries to ensure it captures the required log state. It writes progress and LSN information to the target directory; that metadata is required for the prepare step. For enterprise users there is a commercial counterpart, but for this chapter we focus on XtraBackup because it is widely used and accessible. Think of XtraBackup as a two-part system: a fast file copier and a metadata recorder that together make a consistent prepared image possible.

Before running a backup you must prepare the server and environment. Start by installing Percona XtraBackup 8.0 on the server that runs MySQL 8.0. On Debian or Ubuntu you would use the package manager to install percona-xtrabackup-80; on RHEL or CentOS install the matching package. Next, create a dedicated backup user and grant the required privileges: RELOAD, PROCESS, LOCK TABLES, REPLICATION CLIENT, BINLOG ADMIN, and BACKUP_ADMIN. This separation reduces risk and keeps audit trails clear. Choose a target directory with ample free space—physical backups duplicate data at the filesystem level so the backup destination should be sized at least as large as your data directory plus headroom for the prepare step. Consider filesystem performance: a slow target can prolong backup windows. Finally, verify that the backup user can connect and that the MySQL datadir path you will pass to xtrabackup matches the server's configuration. A common mistake at this stage is assuming default paths; always verify /var/lib/mysql or your custom datadir before proceeding. These preparation steps reduce surprises during the actual backup and ensure the backup will be usable for prepare and restore.

The primary command uses xtrabackup --backup with --target-dir to specify where the files will be saved, --user and --password for the backup user, and --datadir to indicate the live MySQL data directory. Before you move on, keep three core concepts front of mind. First, physical backups copy raw files and log metadata and are the fastest option for large databases, but they require environment compatibility. Second, a hot InnoDB backup captures the LSN and redo logs so a later prepare step can apply committed transactions and make the files consistent. Third, XtraBackup produces metadata files like xtrabackup_binlog_info that you must preserve for point-in-time recovery, and always follow the restore checklist of stopping MySQL, copy-back, fixing permissions, and verifying the data.
